searches.note: Twenty four searches of a share of twenty eight, none of them the author's, four left unspent. The house's own domain was searched twice by restriction (gilfamily.es for the relaunch and the generations, bodegascastano.com for Hécula's height and the organic certificate) and barahonda.com once, each read as primary through its summary; the BOE once (boe.es), read as primary; the DOP Yecla, the Ruta del Vino de Yecla and the ministry twice for the subzone. The rest went to the open web with the author's sources blocked (the houses' domains, El Español, Regal Wine Co, Liberty Wines, European Cellars, Spanish Wine Lover, Rare Wine Co, Olé & Obrigado) so that an independent account could be heard. The four shared searches are the order of 1975 and the subzone Campo Arriba, which serve Castaño and Barahonda both. One fetch tried, of the DOP Yecla pliego on the ministry's host (www.mapa.gob.es), refused because the host is not allowed here, and not retried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites and their heights, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the governing texts (the BOE and the DOP Yecla for the order of 1975 and the subzone), then to independent accounts of each house's dates and people, then to merchants' and importers' sheets of each wine for the blend, the months in oak and the height, the author's sources blocked.

Where the sheets disagreed and none was primary, the figure was hedged as each source's or cut; where a fact rested on one account read by the author and was found nowhere by the refuter (Zona Zepa's 2008, the malolactic in foudres, the slope facing Valtosca), it was taken out.

tested: The founding of 1916, with the house and El Español blocked: Jumilla Wines, Grape Guru and Gourmet Hunters give 1916, and the house's own pages (read through search) give the first harvest and the first bottled wine that year. Borne out. The founder is named two ways (Giménez and Jiménez) and his dates were found nowhere, so he stays described.

The relaunch of 2002: two of the English accounts read (among Jumilla Wines, Grape Guru and i-WineReview) give 2001; the Spanish accounts (Bodeboca, La Esencia del Vino, Revista Gastrónomo) have the relaunch planned by the two brothers in late 2001 and begun in earnest in 2002; the house's own page speaks of the change of millennium and dates to 2002 only the joining of other small bodegas to the group. Changed: the story now tells late 2001 and 2002, and the family no longer dates a new era from 2002. The detail of two months spent on the accounts rests on El Español alone and is cut.

The generations: the founder, his son, his grandson and the grandson's two sons, the Gil Vera brothers, by the Spanish accounts, and Jumilla Wines and Gourmet Hunters make the founder the brothers' great grandfather; the house's own page has the fourth generation at the head in 2016. Grape Collective calls the founder the brothers' grandfather, against the rest. The new story question rests here.

The Silver Label: Monastrell alone, fermented in steel and about twelve months in French oak, by Wine.com (2018 and 2022 listings), Grand Wine Cellar and the house's sheet. Borne out. The first certified organic vintage is 2018 by Wine.com and K&L, 2022 by one shop: the record now hedges it by merchants' listings.
The Blue Label: Monastrell with Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, eighteen months in French and American oak, by Wine.com, Ed's Fine Wines and Vin Chicago. The author's mostly in oak is changed.

The house rules: nobody living named (the brothers, their mother and the El Nido partner are met and described or left out), no price, no score, no volatile figure, British, no dash. The label term Denominación de Origen Protegida Jumilla was printed without a label read, so it becomes the plain Jumilla.

changed.why: Independent accounts give 2001 (two English accounts) or late 2001 into 2002 (the Spanish accounts); the house's page dates no new era to 2002; the accounts detail rests on one newspaper.

tested: The estate's history, with the house and the author's importers blocked: the accounts read (Enterwine, Falstaff, Wine Enthusiast and merchants among them) have the grandfather buy the estate in 1941 (one account 1942), a rosemary and esparto business with an old winery and scattered vines dating to the 1870s, planted by French growers fleeing phylloxera; Enterwine has the son in law propose recovering the old winery in 1991; one account gives 1991 for the first commercial vintage, another 1993 for the first wines on the market. Borne out as told, the 1870s still told as said.

Pie Franco: La Solana planted in 1942 by most listings, 1941 by a few; sandy loam by Wine.com, glacis sediment by another, so sand stands; south west exposure by one listing against the author's south facing, so the aspect is cut. Native yeasts in underground stone lagares with a share of whole bunches by Gourmet Hunters, MoVida and a 2008 review; 500 litre barrels and 5,000 litre foudres for about sixteen months by a 2023 listing. The malolactic in foudres was read nowhere and is cut; well over a year stands.

The other wines: Las Gravas is Monastrell with Garnacha (90 to 92 per cent Monastrell in 2021 and 2023, Syrah as well in 2012) from a steep, stony slope in the Sierra del Molar at about 760 metres; El Molar is Garnacha alone from parcels in the Sierra del Molar. The author's deep gravel facing Valtosca was read nowhere and is changed.
The house rules: the grandfather, his son in law and the grandson are met by name and described; no price, no score, British, no dash. The questions: one right answer each, distractors of one kind.

tested: The founding: Grape Guru, Enterwine and Todowine give 1950, the founder beginning with bulk wine; the family's own bottlings from 1980 or the 1980s by three accounts, one of them saying it opened the door for other producers; the three sons by name in the same results. Borne out. One listing gives 1985 and is an outlier. No dates or death of the founder were read, so he stays described.

The order of 1975: the BOE's summary of the Gazette of 19 June 1975 lists the order of 19 May 1975 regulating the Denominación de Origen Yecla and its Consejo Regulador; the DOP's own page gives the same and says the rules set out a subzone, Campo Arriba, of Monastrell vineyards alone. Borne out; one secondary account gives 15 May, against the BOE.

Hécula: Monastrell alone, fermented in steel, about six months in barrel, mostly French with some American oak, by Enterwine, Vinissimus and the house; about 750 metres on the north side of Yecla by the house's notes and a merchant; the house places Campo Arriba at 700 to 850 metres. The sites line is changed to the wine's own height. The vines' age is given as 35, 40, 50 and 60 to 80 years and stays old vines only.
Organic: the house's blog has the 2019 vintage from organic vineyards and the certificate in February 2021, after the launch; the story is reworded to say so.
Solanera: Monastrell, 65 to 70 per cent by Vinous and Jesmond, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Garnacha Tintorera. About two thirds stands.

The name Hécula: Murgetana (2017) gives it as the literary name the novelist José Luis Castillo-Puche gave Yecla, and finds no ancient name of that form; a wine page calling it the Roman name is not borne out. The house gives no meaning, so the record gives none, as the author left it.

tested: The blend: about seven tenths Monastrell, two tenths Syrah and one tenth Garnacha Tintorera by Decanter's awards listing of 2022 and Murcia Today. Borne out as Monastrell for the larger part.

The oak: three months in French oak by Murcia Today and another listing, as on the house's page for an earlier vintage; eight months by Kenaston and the author's importer. The making now gives both; the two weeks of fermentation, on one sheet, are cut.
The height: 700 to 900 metres by Murcia Today and a merchant. Borne out.

The family: the house's page has Pedro Candela Soriano selling wine from 1850, his son founding a small winery in 1925, the third generation growing it and the fourth founding Bodegas Barahonda in 2006; Grape Experiences gives the 1850 sales and a wine blog of 2013 (a writer's own site, not cited) the winery of 1925; the house's post on twenty years of its winery dates the present building to 2006, as does Murcia Today, while the same blog has the new winery built in 2004. 1925 and 1850 borne out; 2006 hedged as the house's.

Zona Zepa: a single vineyard of own rooted Monastrell planted in 1940 at about 780 metres in Campo Arriba, by Olé & Obrigado and Flaschenpost. The planting of 1940 in the plan belongs to this vineyard, not to the Campo Arriba wine. Its first vintage was found in neither of two searches, the listings beginning with 2012, so 2008 is cut.
The centenary bottling: Monastrell of the 2022 vintage, limited, by the house; no place given in the refuter's reading, so from Campo Arriba is cut.

The subzone: the DOP's own page and the BOE summary carry the order of 19 May 1975; the DOP's page says its rules set out a subzone, Campo Arriba, of Monastrell vineyards alone, and the Ruta del Vino de Yecla lists Yecla Campo Arriba as Monastrell alone. A blend cannot be that, on the evidence read, so the label term is changed to the wine's name.

livingNote: None of these is named in the fragment's prose; the read together agent adds those it judges living to people.json, and the name Antonio Candela is shared by three generations, so a precaution on the bare form is wise. Described, never named, for want of dates in two sources: the founder of Juan Gil (Juan Gil Giménez by the house, Jiménez by a merchant), his son and grandson (Juan Gil Guerrero or Herrero, and Juan Gil González, who died early by one account), the ancestor of 1850 and the founder of 1925 of the Candela family (Pedro Candela Soriano and Antonio Candela García, named by the house), the founder of Castaño and the founder of Olivares. José Luis Castillo-Puche, the novelist of Yecla whose literary name for the town is Hécula, is long dead but his dates were not read here and he is not in the fragment. A wine blog of 2013 under a writer's own name was met in the results and is cited nowhere.
swapNote: The author proposed no swap; in Barahonda's report the author named Zona Zepa or Heredad Candela as possible flagships for the checker to weigh. The refuter refuses both and proposes none: Campo Arriba is the wine by which the house is known abroad, listed by merchants in several markets and at the Decanter World Wine Awards as Campo Arriba Old Vines, which the thin region rule allows as the wine a house is known by, while Zona Zepa is a single vineyard bottled in some 1,400 bottles by two listings, a wine a guest seldom meets; Heredad Candela was not tested. The other four picks stand: Juan Gil's Etiqueta Plata is the house's Silver Label, Casa Castillo's Pie Franco its wine of La Solana, Castaño's Hécula its organic Monastrell, and Olivares Dulce the sweet red the plan names, fortified.
planNotes: juan-gil: answered. 1916 by the house and three independent accounts; the label words Etiqueta Plata at home and Silver Label abroad, with 12 Meses on older listings and left off the record; 2002 stands for the relaunch begun in earnest, planned in late 2001, and the why's "modern era began with in 2002" is fair only as the importers' account of the Silver Label's first vintage; the founder described; El Nido kept out, a separate bodega of the family.

casa-castillo: answered. 1942 for La Solana by the house and most listings, 1941 by a few, kept in a trap; the purchase of 1941 (one account 1942); no founding year, so founded is empty; Las Gravas the other red, with El Molar.

castano: answered in part, and the why needs a change. 1950 by the house and three accounts; the founder's dates were found nowhere, so he is described; Hécula is Monastrell alone in the vintages taught. The why's "Hécula, which takes an old name of Yecla" is not borne out: Murgetana (2017) gives Hécula as the literary name the novelist José Luis Castillo-Puche gave Yecla and finds no ancient name of that form, and the house gives its wine's name no meaning; the why should drop it. The why's "how most drinkers meet the denomination" is the region record's ranking, borne out by no source read.

olivares: answered. The label Olivares Dulce Monastrell, in a 50 cl bottle; fortified, its fermentation stopped by about two per cent neutral alcohol (VVG's and Rare Wine Co's sheets); Hoya de Santa Ana at about 825 metres in the north west of the DO; 1930 by the house, Polaner and The Rare Wine Collection. The why's "late picked and sweet" is fair; it is also fortified.

barahonda: answered, and the why needs a change. The label Barahonda Campo Arriba, sold abroad as Old Vines; the wine the house is known by abroad; 1925 and 1850 by the house and two other accounts. The planting of 1940 the note asks about belongs to Zona Zepa's single vineyard (Olé & Obrigado, Flaschenpost), not to Campo Arriba, whose vines the author's importer dates to plantings of 1987 to 1992; and the why's "old Monastrell from the high north of Yecla" should read a blend led by Monastrell, about seven tenths, with Syrah and Garnacha Tintorera from Campo Arriba.

codexInTension.says: Yecla names two subzones, Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo
codexInTension.read: The DOP Yecla's own page says the rules of 1975 set out one subzone, Campo Arriba, of Monastrell vineyards alone, and the Ruta del Vino de Yecla lists Yecla Campo Arriba as Monastrell alone; Wine-Searcher calls the division into Campo Arriba and Campo Abajo unofficial, and no source read names Campo Abajo as a subzone. Whether the pliego in force keeps Campo Arriba could not be read.
